newsitem.title: UK: Europe crude outlook - winds cushion sellers' fall.
newsitem.headline: Europe crude outlook - winds cushion sellers' fall.

text.p: European spot crudes will soften this week under the weight of poor refinery margins but concern about weather-related disruption to loadings may keep buyers on their toes, traders said.
With most February North Sea crude sold, markets are expected to remain quiet until the latter part of the week when the first March loading programmes are due to be released.

Crude traders said March volumes would be little changed from February, with the exception of Ekofisk, which could see higher output if a pipeline tie-in linking the Fulmar field is completed successfully.
"Everybody's waiting for the programmes but you would expect the differentials to come off a touch," said a trader.
Two cargoes of U.K. Forties traded Friday at Dated Brent +46 cents, down from talk around +50 cents earlier in the week.
Traders said North Sea crudes would have to weaken further given poor refining margins and recent losses on benchmark Brent.
Dated Brent, which lost about 20 cents over the week was pegged around Mar Brent +10/+15 cents on Monday. An eroding paper curve pointed to softer values later this week, dealers said.
The March/April intermonth spread lost about 10 cents last week to trade at +34 cents on Friday.
But the possibility of bad weather disrupting loadings of Brent and other North Sea crudes could encourage sellers to stand firm.
"The balance of feeling is that sellers will have to concede something on differentials but it is still not entirely clear who has the upper hand in this standoff," said one.
Bad weather forced a suspension of berthings at the Sullom Voe Brent terminal last Thursday and offshore loadings at Norway's Gullfaks and Statfjord were halted a day later.

Statfjord operator Statoil on Sunday said offshore loadings had been resumed at the Statfjord complex and production was coming back to normal after stormy weather forced a reduction in output on Friday.
Traders said winds were expected to batter North Sea installations this week again.
"Heavy seas will likely cause shipping delays," said private forecaster Weather Services Corp on Monday.
Plummeting gas oil prices, which lost over $20 a tonne last week, would keep Russian Urals crude and distillate-rich West African crudes under pressure, traders said.

The Black Sea port of Novorossiisk has been closed for most of February due to high winds but Med refiners are in no hurry to buy Urals and at least one has already scaled back runs due to the dismal margins.

Nigerian grades like Forcados and Bonny Medium were also suffering from gas oil's woes. Sellers said Forcados may struggle to hold a 60-cent plus premium to Dated Brent after a deal last week at +65 cents.
"March (loading) programmes show stable volumes but some grades are clearly going to suffer a bit," said a trader.
